system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. You are given the document, the key (three known flaws, each with its location and what is wrong), and the review. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
This paper proposes raising three main-course prices and replacing the mushroom risotto from 1 April. It rests on four claims:
- the increases add about £810 a week (£42,000 a year) in gross profit;
- the risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and should go;
- loyal customers will absorb the increases;
- main-course margin rises to about 71%.

Several parts are sound:
- **The till data are well used.** Table 1's margins and weekly volumes are correct and add up to 1,050 plates.
- **The competitor claim checks out.** All three new prices are below the midpoint of the competitor range: £17.50 vs £17.98, £16.00 vs £16.50, and £28.00 vs £29.50.
- **The £810 a week is the right figure before costs change.** 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2 = £810, and × 52 weeks = £42,120.

However, the risotto decision reverses what Table 1 shows. The projection also ignores the beef price rise that the paper itself reports.

## 1. The risotto has the highest margin, not the lowest

Table 1 gives the risotto an **80% margin, the best on the menu**. The paper and the author's note both say it has the weakest. In cash terms it earns £11.20 a plate, more than the curry (£10.90) or the burger (£10.80).

The proposed replacement is a seasonal special at the same price. Specials currently run at **64%**. At £14.00, a special earns about £8.96 a plate, which loses about **£200 a week** (90 × £2.24) compared with the risotto.

The low volume (90 a week) doesn't mean the dish isn't earning its place. A good vegetarian main also helps a mixed group choose to book. Options:
- **Keep the risotto.** It is the most profitable dish per pound of sales.
- **Replace it only with a dish costed at 80% or better,** and make clear the change is about menu variety, not margin.

## 2. The beef price rise is left out of the projection

Section 4 says beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start. The projection doesn't include it. Two dishes are affected:
- **Sirloin steak (£10.40 food cost).** This cost is mostly beef, so the rise is about £1.10–£1.25 a plate. That cancels most of the £2.00 price increase.
- **Beef burger (£4.20 food cost).** Depending on how much of the cost is beef, the rise is up to £0.50 a plate.

Together that's about **£200–£280 a week** of extra cost. The realistic gain is roughly **£530–£610 a week (£28,000–£32,000 a year)**, not £810. The paper should use the burger's actual beef content from the recipe costings to firm this up.

## 3. Main-course margin is likely around 68%, not 71%

The 71% figure is roughly correct if costs stay where they are and the risotto stays on the menu. With the beef rise and a 64% special in place of the risotto, my rough recalculation puts main-course margin at **about 68%**. That uses a midpoint of about £240 a week for the beef cost, and a guessed price for the existing specials, since the paper doesn't give one. The 70% target is not restored.

## 4. "If volumes hold" needs testing, not assuming

No customer leaving is assumed, but the paper doesn't show how much volume could be lost before the gain disappears:
- **Fish and chips** earns £12.40 a plate after the increase, so selling about **8% fewer** plates (around 25 a week) would wipe out the £310 gain.
- **Steak** has an even narrower margin for error once the beef cost is included.

The assumption also rests on two weak supports:
- **Repeat custom cuts both ways.** 60% of bookings come from repeat guests, and regulars are exactly the customers who notice price changes.
- **Bookings are the wrong measure.** "The 2024 change had no visible effect on bookings" doesn't show whether guests switched to cheaper dishes, ordered fewer extras, or came less often.

## 5. The monitoring plan will be confounded by the season

The plan compares spring weeks with January–February. Restaurant trade usually picks up in spring, so a real drop in demand could be hidden by seasonal growth. Better comparisons:
- **The same weeks last year,** adjusted for any overall change in covers.
- **The share each dish takes of total mains,** which reveals switching between dishes even when totals move.

Agree in advance what the plan triggers. For example: "if fish and chips falls below X% of mains for three weeks, review its price."

## 6. Smaller points

- **"Six trading days a week"** in the recommendation contradicts the Wednesday–Sunday opening hours in Section 2, which is five days. The weekly figures are unaffected, but the error is visible to the owners.
- **The lunch share should be stated** if the paper calls weekday lunch "a small share."
- **Fish prices** are described as volatile but currently average. A short note on what happens to the fish and chips margin if they rise would help.

## On the author's description

| Claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| Risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu" | It has the strongest (80%) |
| "£810 a week… about £42,000 a year" | Correct before the beef rise; about £530–£610 a week after it |
| Margin rises "to about 71%" | About 68% once beef costs and the risotto replacement are included |
| Prices stay below competitor midpoints | Correct |
| "Monitoring… gives us an early warning" | It compares spring with winter and has no trigger |
| Till data, competitor check, supplier information | All genuinely used, though the supplier information doesn't reach the projection |

## Recommendation

The price increases themselves are reasonable and well positioned against competitors. Before the owners approve them:
1. **Drop the risotto removal**, or require any replacement to match its 80% margin.
2. **Include the beef cost rise** in the projection, using actual recipe costings.
3. **Restate the margin forecast** on that basis and show how far it falls short of the 70% target.
4. **Add break-even volumes** for each increased dish.
5. **Fix the monitoring plan** to use last year's spring weeks and dish share of mains, with agreed triggers.
